doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Gettin' There and its changing lyrics
summary: Audre and Amy discuss the thirty-versus-sixty years line.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: This is different. I’ve turned to “Gettin’ There,” that I’ve always liked. “People ask me questions about the way I’ve spent my life, thirty...” Now, see, I’ve changed that to “sixty years in show business.” He put it back to “thirty.” He wrote that when he’d been in show business... “Thirty years in show-biz, only had one wife. Limousines and swimmin’ pools, I didn’t get my share, but I am not down-hearted. I am not down-hearted. I am not down-hearted, but I’m gettin’ there.”
Is that on the last record?
No, that was a while ago.
Yeah. That always gets...that’s a big laugh line.
Is it on this... No, I think, Gettin’ There is the name of...
“No matter how I’m feeling, I still propose a toast, almost successful...
It’s on Ever Since The World Ended, 1987.
That’s a funny one, “...(?)... the world.” Those are later ones.
